kernelIdea: From p ⇒ q you can form q ⇒ p (converse), ¬p ⇒ ¬q (inverse), and ¬q ⇒ ¬p (contrapositive). Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original.

kernels.l1: If you flip a promise around, you do not get the same promise back.
kernels.l2: You can flip a promise around in a few ways. Only one of them keeps the same meaning: swap the two parts and say not to both.
kernels.l3: From an if–then claim you can build three new ones: the converse, the inverse, and the contrapositive. Only the contrapositive always has the same truth value as the claim you started with.
kernels.l4: From "if p then q" you can form three relatives: the converse, the inverse, and the contrapositive. Only the contrapositive says the same thing as the original.
kernels.l5: The converse and inverse of a conditional may fail even when the conditional holds. Only the contrapositive says the same thing as the original.
kernels.l6: Flipping a conditional gives three relatives; only the contrapositive shares its truth table. The converse and inverse match each other, and neither follows from the original.
kernels.l7: Of the three conditionals built by exchanging and negating the parts, only the contrapositive says the same thing. Converse and inverse match each other and are independent of the original.
kernels.l8: Contraposition is an equivalence of the material conditional with itself under the involution ¬; assuming the converse is the formal shape of the fallacy of affirming the consequent.
